{{Short description|Virginia Siouan language}} {{distinguish|text=the [[Saponi language]] of Indonesia}}{{Infobox language | name = Tutelo | map = Tutelo-Saponi lang.png | mapcaption = Tutelo language region prior to [[European colonization of the Americas|European colonization]]. | nativename = {{Lang|tta|Yesá:sahį́}} | states = [[United States]] | region = [[Virginia]], [[West Virginia]]; later [[Pennsylvania]], [[New York (state)|New York]], [[Ontario]] | ethnicity = [[Tutelo people|Tutelo]], [[Saponi people|Saponi]], [[Occaneechi]], [[Manahoac]], [[Monacan people|Monacan]] | extinct = after 1982, with the death of Albert Green | ref = Marianne Mithun, ''The Languages of Native North America'' | familycolor = American | fam1 = [[Siouan languages|Siouan]] | fam2 = [[Western Siouan languages|Western Siouan]] | fam3 = [[Ohio Valley Siouan languages|Ohio Valley Siouan]] | fam4 = Virginia Siouan | iso3 = tta | linglist = tta | glotto = tute1247 | glottorefname = Tutelo | altname = Tutelo-Saponi | revived = {{circa}}2019{{Cite web |last=WRAL |date=2019-05-03 |title=Project attempts to revive dead language of Haliwa-Saponi tribe |url=https://www.wral.com/video/project-attempts-to-revive-dead-language-of-haliwa-saponi-tribe/18363925/ |access-date=2025-02-20 |website=WRAL.com |language=en}} }} '''Tutelo''', also known as '''Tutelo–Saponi''' ({{Langx|tta|Yesá:sahį́|links=no}}{{Cite web |title=Yesa:sahį Language Project |url=https://www.yesasahin.org/ |access-date=2025-02-20 |website=www.yesasahin.org |language=en-US}}{{Cite web |date=2024-11-25 |title=Corey Roberts works to revitalize the Indigenous language Yesa:sahį́ at Elon |url=https://www.elon.edu/u/news/2024/11/25/corey-roberts-works-to-revitalize-the-indigenous-language-yesasahi-at-elon/ |access-date=2025-02-20 |website=Today at Elon |language=en}}), is a member of the Virginian branch of [[Siouan languages]] that were originally spoken in what is now Virginia and West Virginia in the United States. Most Tutelo speakers migrated north to escape warfare. They traveled through North Carolina, Pennsylvania, and New York. In 1753, the Tutelo had joined the Iroquois Confederacy under the sponsorship of the [[Cayuga nation|Cayuga]]. They finally settled in Ontario after the [[American Revolutionary War]] at what is now known as [[Six Nations of the Grand River First Nation]]. [[Nikonha]], the last fluent speaker in Tutelo country, died in 1871 at age 106. The year before, he had managed to impart about 100 words of vocabulary to the ethnologist [[Horatio Hale]], who had visited him at the Six Nations Reserve.Horatio Hale, [https://books.google.com/books?id=W8ZkyiVU8w0C&pg=PA13 "Tutelo Tribe and Language"], ''Proceedings of the American Philosophical Society'' 21, no. 114 (1883){{cite book | title=The Tutelo Language | publisher=Evolution Publishing | author=Hale, Horatio | year=2001 | location=Merchantville | series = American Language Reprints | volume = 23 | isbn=1889758213}} Descendants living at [[Six Nations of the Grand River|Grand River Reserve]] in Ontario spoke Tutelo well into the 20th century. Linguists including Horatio Hale, [[J. N. B. Hewitt]], [[James Owen Dorsey]], [[Leo J. Frachtenberg]], [[Edward Sapir]], [[Frank Speck]], and [[Marianne Mithun]] recorded the language. The last active speakers, a mother and daughter, died in a house fire shortly before Mithun's visit in 1982. The last native speaker, Albert Green, died sometime after that.{{cite book |first=Giulia |last=Oliverio |title=A grammar and dictionary of Tutelo |year=1996 |publisher=University of Kansas |url=https://kuscholarworks.ku.edu/entities/publication/46f6622c-4d2c-4647-a4a5-8781193a72ba |hdl=1808/35976 }}, p. 6–19. == Documentation == Hale published a brief grammar and vocabulary in 1883 and confirmed the language as Siouan through comparisons with [[Dakota language|Dakota]] and [[Hidatsa language|Hidatsa]]. His excitement was considerable to find an ancient Dakotan language, which was once widespread among inland tribes in Virginia, to have been preserved on a predominantly Iroquoian-speaking reserve in Ontario.Robert Vest, 2006, "Letters of Chief Samuel Johns to Frank G Speck". Previously, the only recorded information on the language had been a short list of words and phrases collected by Lieutenant John Fontaine at [[Fort Christanna]] in 1716, and a few assorted terms recorded by colonial sources, such as [[John Lederer]], [[Abraham Wood]], Hugh Jones, and [[William Byrd II]]. Hale noted the testimony of colonial historian [[Robert Beverley, Jr.]] that the dialect of the [[Occaneechi]], believed to be related to Tutelo, was used as a [[lingua franca]] by all the tribes in the region regardless of their first languages, and it was known to the chiefs, "conjurers," and priests of all tribes. These spiritual practitioners used it in their ceremonies, just as Roman Catholic priests in Europe and the US used [[Latin]]. Hale's grammar also noted further comparisons to Latin and [[Ancient Greek]]. He remarked on the classical nature of Tutelo's rich variety of verb tenses available to the speaker, including what he remarked as an "[[aorist]]" perfect verb tense, ending in {{lang|tta|-wa}}. James Dorsey, another Siouan linguist, collected extensive vocabulary and grammar samples around the same time as Hale, as did Hewitt a few years later. Frachtenberg and Sapir both visited the Six Nations Ontario reserve in the first decade of the 1900s and found that only a few Cayuga of Tutelo ancestry remembered a handful of Tutelo words. Speck did much fieldwork to record and preserve their cultural traditions in the 1930s but found little of the speech remaining. Mithun managed to collect a handful of terms that were still remembered in 1980. The language as preserved by these efforts is now believed to have been mutually intelligible with, if not identical to, the speech of other Virginia Siouan groups in general, including the [[Monacan (tribe)|Monacan]] and [[Manahoac]] and Nahyssan confederacies, as well as the subdivisions of Occaneechi, Saponi, etc. In 1996, Giulia Oliverio wrote ''A Grammar and Dictionary of Tutelo'' as her dissertation.{{Harvsp|Oliverio|1996}} In 2021 the [[Living Tongues Institute for Endangered Languages]] assisted Tutelo activists in building a Living Dictionary for Tutelo-Saponi Monacan.{{cite web |title=The Team Building the Tutelo-Saponi Monacan Living Dictionary Receives A Grant from Native Voices Endowment |url=https://livingtongues.org/tutelo-saponi-monacan-grant/ |website=Living Tongues Institute for Endangered Languages |access-date=11 March 2024}} ==Phonology== Oliverio proposes the following analysis of the sound system of Tutelo:{{Harvsp|Oliverio|1996}}. ===Consonants=== {| class="wikitable" ! colspan="2" | ! style="text-align: center;" | [[labial consonant|Labial]] ! style="text-align: center;" | [[dental consonant|Dental]] ! style="text-align: center;" | [[palatal consonant|Palatal]] ! style="text-align: center;" | [[velar consonant|Velar]] ! style="text-align: center;" | [[glottal consonant|Glottal]] |- ! rowspan="2" | [[plosive consonant|Plosive/

[[low vowel|Low]] | style="text-align: center;" | | style="text-align: center;" | | style="text-align: center;" | {{IPA link|ã}} | style="text-align: center;" | {{IPA link|ãː}} | style="text-align: center;" | | style="text-align: center;" | |} ==Grammar== Independent personal pronouns, as recorded by Dorsey, are: * 1st sing. - {{lang|tta|Mima}} (I) * 2nd sing. - {{lang|tta|Yima}} (you) * 3rd sing. - {{lang|tta|Ima}} (he, she, it) The pronoun {{lang|tta|Huk}} "all" may be added to form the plurals {{lang|tta|Mimahuk}} 'we' and {{lang|tta|Yimahuk}} 'ye', and 'they' is {{lang|tta|Imahese}}. In verbal conjugations, the subject pronouns are represented by various prefixes and suffixes, usually as follows: * 1st sing. - {{lang|tta|Ma-}} or {{lang|tta|Wa-}} (or {{lang|tta|-ma-}}, {{lang|tta|-wa-}}) * 2nd sing. - {{lang|tta|Ya-}} ({{lang|tta|-ya-}}) * 3rd sing. - (null; no affixes, simple verb) * 1st plur. - {{lang|tta|Mank-}} or {{lang|tta|Wa'en-}} (prefix only) * 2nd plur. - {{lang|tta|Ya-}} ({{lang|tta|-ya-}}) + -{{lang|tta|pui}} * 3rd plur. - -{{lang|tta|-hle}}, {{lang|tta|-hne}}. An example as given by Hale is the verb {{lang|tta|Yandosteka}} 'love', and the pronoun is between {{lang|tta|yando-}} and {{lang|tta|-steka}}: *{{lang|tta|Yandowasteka}}, I love *{{lang|tta|Yandoyasteka}}, you love *{{lang|tta|Yandosteka}}, he or she loves *{{lang|tta|Mankyandosteka}}, we love *{{lang|tta|Yandoyastekapui}}, ye love *{{lang|tta|Yandostekahnese}}, they love. The last form includes the common additional tense suffix {{lang|tta|-se}}, which literally conveys the progressive tense. There are also 'stative' classes of verbs that take the 'passive' (oblique) pronoun affixes ({{lang|tta|mi-}} or {{lang|tta|wi-}}, {{lang|tta|yi-}} etc.) as subjects. Additional tenses can be formed by the use of other suffixes including {{lang|tta|-ka}} (past), {{lang|tta|-ta}} (future), {{lang|tta|-wa}} (aorist or perfect), {{lang|tta|-kewa}} (past perfect), and {{lang|tta|-ma}} (perfect progressive).
